**Special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs)** are "blank check" companies: an IPO without an operating business, raising capital first, then seeking a target. SPACs shift IPO risk and expense; the 2015-2020 study cited reports SPAC mergers averaged a -18.8 per cent return versus a +37.2 per cent average for traditional IPOs (Ch 12.1, "Alternative Methods of Raising Capital"). The text suggests SPACs benefit private firm owners (better negotiated price) but harm public-market investors who hold the SPAC.

### Inflation, bond returns, and stock returns

Inflation redistributes wealth: lenders making fixed-rate loans receive less-valuable dollars; borrowers repay with the same; consumers on fixed income suffer. Modest inflation can benefit a consumer-driven economy by motivating spending; high inflation harms it (Ch 12.2, "Inflation Impacts").

Average annual returns by asset class for 1981-2020 (from Aswath Damodaran data):

| Asset class | Nominal average annual return | Standard deviation of returns |
|---|---|---|
| Large company stocks | 12.64% | 16.06% |
| Baa bonds | 10.34% | 7.67% |
| 10-year T-bonds | 8.21% | 9.92% |
| US T-bills | 3.94% | 3.39% |
| Inflation | 2.93% | 1.76% |

(Ch 12.4, Table 12.4)

A $100 invested in 1928 in large-company stocks grew to over 50 times the value of the same $100 invested in long-term US government bonds (Ch 12.4). This supports asset allocation as more important than security selection. Small-cap stocks historically outperformed large-cap, but the differential has narrowed since 1980 (12.13 per cent vs 11.82 per cent compounded annual return for Wilshire small-cap vs large-cap, 1980-2020).

The section's Link to Learning box "Does It Pay to Time the Market?" puts a figure on the cost of missing the market's best days. An investment of $10,000 in an S&P 500 index fund over 1980 to mid-2020 would have grown to $697,421; missing the 5 best-performing days would have cut the final balance to $432,411, and staying out on the 10 best days would have left $313,377 [AP], "or less than half of the return earned in the full time period" [V] (Ch 12.4, "Does It Pay to Time the Market?").

A second Link to Learning box, "Does It Pay to Invest Globally?", relays a review of global stock market returns from 1900 to 2020 built on data by Elroy Dimson, Paul Marsh and Mike Staunton for Credit Suisse [BT, Steiner; Dimson, Marsh and Staunton]. US equity markets have been among the highest performing since 1900, with only Australia showing a higher average annual return over the 121 years, and over the period the United States benefited from an entrepreneurial spirit and its distance from the centre of two world wars [BT, Steiner; Dimson, Marsh and Staunton]. Most established economies have not out-returned US equities but they offer diversification, and "the greatest return potential—and the greatest risk of loss—may lie in developing economies" [V]; investing experts do not fully agree on the merits of foreign equity markets [AP] (Ch 12.4, "Does It Pay to Invest Globally?").

### Profiles cited

Three profile sidebars are presented in the chapter: Janet Yellen (career path through Federal Reserve, first woman Fed chair, first woman Treasury Secretary), Bill Gross (cofounder of Pimco, "the bond king," focus on total returns rather than yield), and Warren Buffett (career, investment philosophy, philanthropy) (Ch 12.2, 12.3, 12.4).

## Part XIII: Statistical analysis in finance (Ch 13)

### Measures of centre

**Arithmetic mean** is the most common measure of average; sum of values divided by count [AP] (Ch 13.1, "Arithmetic Mean"). The **median** is the middle value of an ordered data set; preferred when outliers are present because it is insensitive to extreme values (Ch 13.1, "Median"). Its position in the ordered data comes from an expression in n, the number of data values: with an odd n the median is the middle value, with an even n it is the two middle values added together and divided by 2; for the five Treasury bill auction amounts of Table 13.1 it is the third value, $39.7 billion [AP] (Ch 13.1, "Median"). A Think It Through example makes the outlier point: in a village of 50 where 49 people earn $30,000 and one earns $5 million, the median of $30,000 is the better measure of centre [AE] because it "gives us a better sense of the middle of the data set" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Finding the Measure of Center"). The **mode** is the most frequent value (Ch 13.1, "Mode"). The **geometric mean** "redistributes not the sum of the values but their product"; it is the nth root of the product of n values; used for compound growth rates such as multi-period returns [AP] (Ch 13.1, "Geometric Mean"). The **weighted mean** assigns different weights to different values; common application is computing the average purchase price of a stock acquired at different prices in different quantities (Ch 13.1, "Weighted Mean").

### Measures of spread

The **standard deviation** measures how far data values are from the mean; finance uses it as a primary measure of volatility and therefore risk [AP] (Ch 13.2, "Standard Deviation"). Sample and population formulas differ: the sample uses n-1 in the denominator. The text sets out a nine-step method for a sample: find the mean; tabulate each data value's difference from the mean (these differences sum to zero); square each difference; add the squares; divide the sum by n-1 to get the sample variance s²; take its square root for the sample standard deviation s; and round both to one more decimal place than the data values [AP] (Ch 13.2, "Variance"). **Variance** is the square of the standard deviation; the standard deviation is in the same units as the underlying data, making it more interpretable.

### Measures of position

A **z-score (z-value)** is `(x - μ) / σ`; it expresses the number of standard deviations a value is from the mean (Ch 13.3, "z-Scores"). **Quartiles** divide ordered data into quarters; the first, second (median), and third quartiles correspond to the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles. The **interquartile range (IQR)** is Q3 - Q1; the IQR is used to flag potential outliers — values below Q1 - 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR are typically flagged (Ch 13.3, "Outlier Detection").

Two Think It Through examples apply these measures. In "Interpreting a z-Score", a technology-based mutual fund's 12.4% return, against a 7.8% mean and a 2.3% standard deviation for comparable funds, lies 2 standard deviations above the mean, "indicating that this mutual fund generated a significantly better rate of return than all other technology-based mutual funds for the same time period" [V] [AE] (Ch 13.3, "Interpreting a z-Score"). In "Calculating the IQR", of 13 portfolio values only $5,500,000 lies beyond the outlier bounds (above 1,159,375), so it is flagged as a potential outlier, which matters because "the presence of outliers could potentially indicate data errors or some other anomalies in the data set that should be investigated" [V] [AE] (Ch 13.3, "Calculating the IQR").

### Distributions and expected value

The **normal distribution** is the foundational continuous distribution in finance; it is symmetric about the mean, with mean = median = mode. Its parameters are the mean μ and the standard deviation σ. Excel's `NORM.DIST(x, μ, σ, TRUE)` returns the area under the curve to the left of x — i.e., the probability that a value falls below x (Ch 13.4, "Normal Distribution"). The **exponential distribution** is one with fewer large values and more small values; common in modelling time-to-event problems such as time-to-default, customer-spending distribution, or product-reliability lifetimes (Ch 13.4, "Exponential Distribution"). Probabilities come from areas under the exponential curve, using a formula for the area to the left of a given value [AP]; a Think It Through example applies it to the time between incoming phone calls at a financial company, with a mean of 45 seconds (0.75 minutes) [AE] (the question asks for 2 minutes or less between calls; the solution takes the area to the left of 1 minute) (Ch 13.4, "Calculating Probability").

A **probability distribution** assigns probabilities to outcomes; **expected value** of a probability distribution is the weighted mean where probabilities are the weights: `E[R] = Σ Pᵢ × Rᵢ` [AP] (Ch 13.5, "Calculate and Interpret Expected Values"). In portfolio analysis, weights by asset category (stocks, bonds, cash equivalents) are determined by dividing each category's value by total portfolio value; portfolio rebalancing brings actual weights to target weights (Ch 13.5, "Calculate Portfolio Weights").

For normally distributed data the **empirical rule** gives areas under the curve: about 68% of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two and about 99.7% within three, so almost all values lie within three standard deviations of the mean [AP] (Ch 13.5, "Apply the Normal Distribution in Financial Contexts").

## Part XIV: Regression analysis in finance (Ch 14)

### Correlation

**Correlation** is the measure of association between two numeric variables (Ch 14.1, "Calculate a Correlation Coefficient"). The **correlation coefficient (r)**, developed by Karl Pearson, is the strength and direction of linear correlation. Its value lies between -1 and +1; +1 is perfect positive correlation, -1 is perfect negative correlation, 0 is no linear correlation; in both perfect cases all the original data points lie on a straight line, and the size of r indicates the strength of the linear relationship [AP] (Ch 14.1, "Interpret a Correlation Coefficient"). The text takes a position: "correlation does not imply causation" [V] (Ch 14.1).

The text gives a quick rule for testing significance: if r exceeds `2/√n`, the correlation between the two variables is statistically significant at approximately the 0.05 level; with 10 observations the threshold is 0.6325, with 30 observations it is 0.3651, with 100 observations it is 0.2000 (Ch 14.1, "Test a Correlation Coefficient for Significance"). The formal hypothesis test sets the null hypothesis that the population correlation coefficient is not significantly different from zero (no significant linear relationship between x and y in the population) against the alternative that it is significantly different from zero [AP] (Ch 14.1, "Test a Correlation Coefficient for Significance"). In a Think It Through example, a CFO finds a correlation of -0.68 between stock prices and the unemployment rate over 10 years (10 data points); because the absolute value of r exceeds the threshold of about 0.632, the correlation is deemed significant at the 0.05 level [AE] (Ch 14.1, "Determining If a Correlation Is Significant").

### Linear regression

**Linear regression** uses the **method of least squares** to find a best-fit line that minimises the sum of squared residuals (the differences between observed y-values and predicted ŷ-values) [AP] (Ch 14.2, "Method of Least Squares and Residuals"). In the regression equation b is the slope and a the y-intercept, and ŷ ("y-hat") is the predicted value of the dependent variable y for a given value of the independent variable x; depending on the slope, the line slopes upward to the right, is horizontal, or slopes downward to the right (Figure 14.3) [AP] (Ch 14.2, "Method of Least Squares and Residuals"). Five assumptions underlie the test of significance for linear regression (Ch 14.2, "Assumptions for Linear Regression"):

1. There is a linear relationship in the population.
2. The y-values for any particular x-value are normally distributed about the line.
3. The standard deviations of population y-values are equal across x-values.
4. The residual errors are mutually independent.
5. The data are produced from a well-designed random sample or randomised experiment.

### Applications in finance

Regression analysis underpins the calculation of a stock's **beta**, regressing stock returns on market returns. Beta is the slope of the regression line and measures systematic risk. Regression also produces **prediction intervals** (Ch 14.5) — interval estimates of where a future observation is likely to fall. The prediction interval for an individual y is computed from the standard deviation of the error term (se), the standard deviation of the x-variable (sx) and a critical value of the t-distribution [AP] (Ch 14.5, "Generating Prediction Intervals"). As the x chosen for prediction moves further from the central weight of the data, the interval widens even at a constant confidence level, which shows that "the precision of any estimate will diminish as one tries to predict beyond the largest weight of the data" [V] (Ch 14.5, "Generating Prediction Intervals"; Figure 14.12). Excel's SLOPE and INTERCEPT functions, or the chart trendline tool, perform the regression directly. The **R statistical software** is named as an open alternative beyond Excel (Ch 14.6).

## Part XV: How to think about investing — risk, return, CAPM (Ch 15)

### Realised return and average return

The **realised return** of an investment over a holding period is `(Final Value + Dividends - Initial Value) / Initial Value` [AP] (Ch 15.1, "Individual Investment Realized Return"). The **dividend yield** is dividends received divided by the initial price; the **capital gain yield** is the change in price divided by the initial price; total percent return is their sum. A Think It Through example (10 shares of 3M bought at $175, $5.91 a share in dividends, sold at $169.72) gives a 3.38% dividend yield and a negative capital gain, "often referred to as a capital loss" [V]; the total dollar return stays positive because of the dividend income [AE] (Ch 15.1, "Calculating Return"). The **effective annual rate (EAR)** annualises a holding-period return: `EAR = (1 + holding-period return)^(periods per year) - 1`.

The **arithmetic average return** is the mean of single-period returns; the **geometric average return** is the compounded annual return: `((1+R₁)(1+R₂)...(1+Rₙ))^(1/n) - 1`. The geometric average is always less than or equal to the arithmetic average; the two are equal only if all returns are identical [AP] (Ch 15.1, "Average Annual Returns"). The text takes a position: the geometric average tells you what you actually earned per year on average compounded; the arithmetic average tells you what you earned in a typical year. "When we are looking at the historical description of the distribution of returns and want to predict what to expect in a particular year, the arithmetic average is the relevant calculation" [V] (Ch 15.1).

### Volatility, firm-specific risk, and diversification

Volatility of returns is measured by standard deviation; in finance, this is risk [AP] (Ch 15.1, "Volatility of Returns"). Risk has two components (Ch 15.2):

- **Firm-specific risk (unsystematic, diversifiable risk)**: events affecting one company's revenue or costs (a product liability lawsuit, a new product, accounting irregularities). Diversification eliminates this risk.
- **Systematic risk (market risk)**: events affecting the overall market (Federal Reserve actions, geopolitical events, pandemics). Diversification does not eliminate this risk.

Per research by Meir Statman, a portfolio's standard deviation drops quickly as the number of stocks rises from one to two or three, and each further stock reduces risk by less [BT] (Ch 15.2, "Portfolio Size and Risk"); below a certain level, portfolio risk does not drop however diversified the portfolio becomes (Ch 15.2). On how many stocks make a well-diversified portfolio, "There is not an exact number that all financial managers agree on" [V]; the text's own view is that "the average investor can create a reasonably diversified portfolio with approximately a dozen stocks" [V] (Ch 15.2, "Portfolio Size and Risk"). The benefit of diversification is greatest when stocks have low correlation; the 2011-2020 example shows DAL (Delta) and LUV (Southwest) at 0.87 correlation — both airlines, much diversification benefit lost — versus DAL and XOM (ExxonMobil) at 0.35.

The Link to Learning box "Peloton and Risk" draws on press sources [BT, Trefis; Kilgore] for an example of how news can move a stock price. On May 5, 2021, Peloton recalled all of its Tread+ and Tread products after the death of a child and 70 injuries associated with their use; the stock, at $96.70 a share the previous day, dropped approximately 15% when the recall was announced and closed at $82.62 [BT, Trefis; Kilgore] (Ch 15.1, "Peloton and Risk").

The section's Link to Learning box "How to Build a Diversified Portfolio" relays the advice of TV personality, former hedge fund manager and author Jim Cramer [BT, Stevenson]: build a diversified portfolio with no more than 20% of it in one sector, by buying five to 10 stocks [BT, Stevenson] (Ch 15.2, "How to Build a Diversified Portfolio").

### Risk-free rate, risk premium, and beta

The **risk-free rate** is the return on a default-risk-free investment, typically proxied by short-term US Treasury securities; the average three-month T-bill return for 1928-2020 was 3.36 per cent [V] (Ch 15.3, "Risk-Free Rate"). The **risk premium** is the extra return earned for taking on risk; the average S&P 500 return for 1928-2020 was 11.64 per cent, implying a market risk premium of 8.28 per cent [V] (Ch 15.3, "Risk Premium").

**Beta**: "The measure of how much a stock moves with the market is known as its beta" [V]; it measures the stock's systematic risk [AP] (Ch 15.3, "Beta"). A beta of 1 means the stock moves in step with the market; greater than 1 means more pronounced moves than the market; less than 1 means smaller moves. Beta is calculated as the slope of the regression line of stock returns on market returns.

### The CAPM equation

The **capital asset pricing model (CAPM)** is the asset-pricing model based on the idea that investors are rewarded for systematic risk only; firm-specific risk can be diversified away [AR] (Ch 15.3, "The Capital Asset Pricing Model"). The CAPM equation is:

`Re = Rf + β × (Rm - Rf)`

where Re is the expected return of the asset, Rf is the risk-free rate, β is the asset's beta, and (Rm - Rf) is the market risk premium.

The section's Link to Learning box "Calculating Beta" notes that data providers list company betas but do not always agree: in early February 2021 Yahoo! Finance reported DAL's beta as 1.46 and MarketWatch as 1.29 [BT, Yahoo! Finance; MarketWatch], both slightly different from the 1.39 the text calculates from three years of monthly DAL and S&P 500 returns (Figure 15.3) [AP]. It gives three reasons betas vary from source to source: the time frame used (three to five years is common), the frequency of the data (monthly or weekly returns), and the measure of the market return (the S&P 500 is one of the most common, but alternatives exist) [AP] (Ch 15.3, "Calculating Beta").

### Performance measurement

Three measures of investment performance are catalogued (Ch 15.4):

- **Sharpe ratio**: `(Rp - Rf) / σp`; portfolio risk premium divided by portfolio standard deviation. A reward-to-risk measure of total risk, developed by Nobel laureate William F. Sharpe [AP] (Ch 15.4, "Sharpe Ratio").
- **Treynor ratio**: `(Rp - Rf) / βp`; portfolio risk premium divided by portfolio beta. A reward-to-risk measure of systematic risk.
- **Jensen's alpha**: portfolio's actual return minus the CAPM-predicted return. A positive alpha indicates abnormal positive performance.

Sharpe and Treynor are relative measures; alpha is an absolute measure of abnormal return.

A Think It Through example compares two managers over 10 years in which the US Treasury rate averaged 2% and the S&P 500 return 11%: Mr. Wong (14% average return, 8% standard deviation, beta 1.2) and Ms. Petrov (16%, 10%, beta 1.6). All three measures (Sharpe, Treynor and Jensen's alpha) favour Mr. Wong: "Although Ms. Petrov has had a larger average return, the portfolio she manages is riskier" [V]. The CAPM puts the expected return for a beta of 1.6 at 16.4%, so investors in Ms. Petrov's portfolio were not rewarded for the risk they took as much as would be expected [AE] (Ch 15.4, "Comparing the Returns and Risks of Portfolios").

## Part XVI: How companies think about investing — capital budgeting (Ch 16)

### Payback period

The **payback period** is the time it takes for a company to make enough free cash flow from a project to recover the initial cost [AP] (Ch 16.1, "Payback Period Calculation"). Its principal advantage is simplicity. Its disadvantages: it ignores the time value of money, has no theoretically grounded acceptance criterion (the chosen target is arbitrary), ignores cash flows after the breakeven point, and makes no risk adjustment.

A Link to Learning feature, "Calculating the Payback Period", adds that a project may not fully recover its initial cost in one year yet more than recover it by the following year; in such cases "the payback period will not be an integer but will contain a fraction of a year" [V]. The feature points to a video showing the calculation (Ch 16.1, "Calculating the Payback Period").

### Net present value (NPV)

**Net present value (NPV)** is "the difference between the present value of the cash inflows and the present value of cash outflows" [V] (Ch 16.2, "NPV Calculation"). The decision criterion is grounded in financial theory: accept projects with positive NPV (which add value to the firm) and reject those with negative NPV. NPV uses the firm's cost of capital as the discount rate; the discount rate "can be increased or decreased to adjust for the riskiness of the project's cash flows" [V] (Ch 16.2, "Advantages").

A Link to Learning feature, "Calculating the NPV of an MBA Program", presents NPV as "a decision tool when you are deciding whether you should spend money today to make money in the future" [V]. It points to a website that computes the NPV of an MBA degree, where the initial cost includes both tuition and the wages a full-time student could have earned if not in school [AE] (Ch 16.2, "Calculating the NPV of an MBA Program").

The **NPV profile** plots NPV against discount rate. Where the profile crosses the horizontal axis (NPV = 0), the discount rate equals the project's IRR; this also bounds the firm's allowable cost of capital (Ch 16.2, "NPV Profile").

The text takes positions: the NPV method "provides a criterion for whether or not a project is a good project" but "does not always provide a good solution when a company must make a choice between several acceptable projects because funds are not available to pursue them all" [V] (Ch 16.2, "Disadvantages").

### Internal rate of return (IRR)

The **internal rate of return (IRR)** is "the discount rate that sets the present value of the cash inflows equal to the present value of the cash outflows" [V]; equivalently, the discount rate at which NPV equals zero [AP] (Ch 16.3, "Internal Rate of Return (IRR) Calculation"). The decision rule: accept projects whose IRR exceeds the cost of capital; reject those whose IRR is below. The text catalogues three disadvantages (Ch 16.3, "Disadvantages"):

- **No single mathematical solution** when negative cash flows occur in more than one period — multiple IRRs may exist.
- **Reinvestment rate assumption**: IRR assumes intermediate cash flows are reinvested at the IRR itself, which may not be feasible if the IRR is high.
- **Overlooking differences in scale**: IRR is a percentage and ignores absolute magnitudes; it cannot rank projects of different sizes.

### Alternative methods

The **profitability index (PI)** is the present value of inflows divided by the present value of outflows [AP] (Ch 16.4, "Profitability Index"). PI uses the same inputs as NPV but expresses them as a ratio; it is useful for ranking projects under capital constraints. PI > 1 means accept; PI < 1 means reject (consistent with NPV).

The **discounted payback period** discounts the cash flows before computing the payback period; addresses the time-value flaw of the simple payback period but retains its other limitations (Ch 16.4, "Discounted Payback Period").

The **modified internal rate of return (MIRR)** finds the discount rate that equates the present value of outflows to the future value (terminal value) of inflows compounded at the firm's cost of capital. MIRR resolves IRR's reinvestment-rate assumption and multiple-solution problems but cannot rank projects across different scales (Ch 16.4, "Modified Internal Rate of Return").

### Choosing between projects

For **mutually exclusive projects** (projects that compete so that choosing one excludes the others), the rule is to take the project with the highest NPV (not the highest IRR or the shortest payback) [AR] (Ch 16.5, "Choosing between Mutually Exclusive Projects"). In the worked example, Sam's Sporting Goods compares its original $16,000 embroidery machine with a $25,000 heavy-duty machine that generates more cash inflow in years 3 to 6. Both have a positive NPV and an IRR above the 9 per cent cost of capital, but the regular machine has the higher IRR (14.10 per cent against 13.20 per cent) and the heavy-duty machine the higher NPV ($3,970.67 against $2,835.62) [AE] (Ch 16.5, Table 16.11). Because NPV estimates the value a project creates, "choosing the project with the higher NPV is choosing the project that will create the greater value" [V] (Ch 16.5, "Choosing between Mutually Exclusive Projects").

A Link to Learning feature, "Olympic Project Economics", notes that government entities use the same investment analysis procedures as companies [AP]. Olympic host cities receive direct revenues from broadcast rights, ticket sales and licensing agreements, and expect indirect benefits from tourism, including employment and tax revenues, but only after a major investment in stadiums, housing and transportation [AE]. The infrastructure investment for the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi, Russia, exceeded $50 billion [BT, Filipov] (Ch 16.5, "Olympic Project Economics").

For projects with **different lives**, two methods correct for unequal horizons (Ch 16.5, "Choosing between Projects with Different Lives"):

- **Replacement chain approach**: assume the short project is repeated as many times as needed to match the long project's life, then compare NPVs.
- **Equal annuity approach**: convert each project's NPV into an equivalent annuity payment (a payment that, if received continuously, would have the same NPV); the project with the higher annuity is preferred. In the ice-cream truck example (10 per cent cost of capital), the three-year older truck's NPV of $49,474 converts to a three-year annuity of $19,894 and the six-year newer truck's NPV of $80,658 to a six-year annuity of $18,520; with these annuities valued as perpetuities, the older, larger truck is again preferred, as under the replacement chain [AE] (Ch 16.5, "Equal Annuity Approach").

Both methods assume projects can be replicated; this is not always realistic and errors compound over longer horizons.

For **resource-constrained capital budgeting** (more good projects than capital), rank projects by profitability index and select highest PI first until the budget is exhausted. Ranking by NPV alone produces inferior outcomes when project sizes differ (Ch 16.5, "Choosing Projects When Resources Are Limited").

The chapter closes with an honesty note: NPV calculations are based on projected cash flows that are estimates. "A project that has a positive NPV and is accepted when a company is planning how to allocate its capital toward investments may end up being a bad project that the company wishes it had avoided if the future is much different from what it projected" [V] (Ch 16.5, "Capital Budgeting Challenges"). The 2020 oil-price collapse during the COVID-19 pandemic is given as an example of how cash flows can deviate dramatically from projections.

A Link to Learning feature, "Reducing Capital Spending", reports a June 2020 McKinsey & Company look at major companies worldwide that were cutting their 2020 capital budgets by 10 to 80 per cent from planned levels in the face of the COVID-19 pandemic [BT, Brinded; Cutler; Kok; Parbhoo]. Cuts were especially large in oil and gas, where falling revenue projections drove down the NPV of planned projects, and companies also needed to free up cash: with more limited cash, "fewer positive NPV projects could be accepted and funded" [V] (Ch 16.5, "Reducing Capital Spending").

### Capital budgeting in Excel

Excel's NPV function "calculates the sum of the present values of the cash flows occurring from period 1 through the end of the project using the designated discount rate, but it fails to include the initial investment at time period zero" [V] (Ch 16.6, "Calculating NPV Using Excel"). The user must "include references only to the cells that contain cash flows from year 1 to the end of the project. Then, subtract the initial investment of year 0" [V] to get NPV by its standard definition (Ch 16.6). The IRR function, unlike NPV, uses all of the project's cash flows, including the initial outflow at time 0 (Ch 16.6, "Calculating IRR Using Excel").

## Part XVII: Capital structure and the cost of capital (Ch 17)

### Capital structure and weights

A firm's **capital structure** is "the relative proportions of debt and equity that a firm uses in financing its assets" [AP] (Ch 17.1, "The Basic Balance Sheet"). Debt is referred to as **financial leverage**. Capital has an opportunity cost: "providing a return equal to what potential investors could expect to earn elsewhere for a similar risk is the cost a company bears in exchange for obtaining funds from investors" [V] (Ch 17.1, "Attracting Capital"). The **weighted average cost of capital (WACC)** is the firm's overall cost of capital, weighted by the market-value proportions of each financing source.

Weights are derived from current market values, not book values, on a market-value-based balance sheet (Ch 17.1, "Weights in the Capital Structure").

### Cost of debt capital

A firm's cost of debt is the YTM on its existing debt — the interest rate it would have to pay to refinance. The **after-tax cost of debt** is `Rd × (1 - T)`, where Rd is the YTM and T is the corporate tax rate [AP] (Ch 17.2, "After-Tax Cost of Debt"). Interest is tax-deductible, so the effective cost is lower than the rate paid to lenders. The text catalogues the example of Bluebonnet Industries: 6 per cent coupon bonds selling at 97 per cent of face value with 15 years to maturity yield 6.312 per cent before tax; at a 21 per cent corporate tax rate, the after-tax cost is 4.99 per cent.

### Cost of equity capital

Two methods estimate the cost of equity capital (Ch 17.2, "Cost of Equity Capital"):

- **CAPM**: Re = Rf + β(Rm - Rf). In the Bluebonnet example (equity beta 1.3, a 3 per cent 10-year Treasury-note rate as the risk-free proxy, an 11 per cent long-run market return), the 8 per cent market risk premium means stock-market investors are "paid 8% more than they would have been paid if they had purchased US Treasury notes" [V] (Ch 17.2, "CAPM"). Requires assumptions about the risk-free rate, the market risk premium (typically 5-8 per cent), and the firm's beta. The text catalogues a range of beta estimates from MarketWatch and Yahoo! Finance; for some firms, the two sources yield estimates of equity cost of capital that differ by more than a factor of two (Ch 17.3, "Estimating the Equity Cost of Capital", Table 17.3). For Goodyear Tire and Rubber, MarketWatch's beta of 1.24 and Yahoo! Finance's beta of 2.26 leave "an estimate of the equity cost of capital between 9.20% and 21.08%, using a range of reasonable assumptions" [V] (Ch 17.3).
- **Constant dividend growth model**: Re = D₁/P₀ + g. Requires assumptions about next year's dividend and the dividend growth rate. Cannot be used for non-dividend-paying companies. A Think It Through feature, "Using the Constant Dividend Growth Model", shows that a higher share price, other inputs held constant, implies a lower equity cost of capital: if Bluebonnet's price rises from $12.50 to $16.50 per share with no expected change in dividend growth, the estimate "drops to 11.27%" [V] (Ch 17.2, "Using the Constant Dividend Growth Model").

### WACC

The full WACC formula:

`WACC = D% × Rd × (1 - T) + P% × Rp + E% × Re`

where D%, P%, E% are the weights of debt, preferred stock, and common equity, which must sum to 100 per cent because the company must account for all of its financing [AP]; Rd is the before-tax cost of debt; Rp is the cost of preferred stock; and Re is the cost of common equity (Ch 17.3, "WACC Equation"). For firms without preferred stock, P% = 0.

**Net debt** is total debt minus cash and cash equivalents; many practitioners use net debt rather than total debt when calculating WACC weights, especially for firms holding substantial cash reserves (Ch 17.3, "Net Debt").

### Capital structure choices: MM Proposition II and the impact of taxes

In a perfect-capital-markets benchmark with no taxes, the choice of capital structure does not affect firm value. As leverage increases, the equity beta and equity cost of capital rise proportionally to offset the lower cost of debt, leaving WACC constant. This result is **MM Proposition II**: `Re = Ru + (D/E)(Ru - Rd)`, where Ru is the cost of equity for an unlevered firm [BT] (Ch 17.4, "Leverage and the WACC").

The section's worked example, a one-year T-shirt business costing $40,000, distinguishes **unlevered equity**, the equity in a firm with no financial leverage, from **levered equity**, the equity a firm raises when it also has debt [AP] (Ch 17.4, "The Unlevered Firm"; "The Levered Firm"). Financing $17,000 of the cost with risk-free debt at 4 per cent leaves the firm's value at $45,614, because the expected cash flows "are determined by the productivity of its assets, not the manner in which those assets are financed" [V] (Ch 17.4, "The Levered Firm").

A Link to Learning feature, "MM Proposition I", credits Nobel laureates Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller with influential papers on capital structure and the cost of capital that began from a perfectly competitive market, one of whose assumptions is that there are no taxes [BT, Modigliani; Miller]. The idea that "the market value of the unlevered and levered firm is the same in perfect capital markets" [V] is known as MM Proposition I; the feature points to the Milken Institute's 5-Minute Finance site for more (Ch 17.4, "MM Proposition I").

In the real world, taxes break the irrelevance result. Interest is tax-deductible, generating an **interest tax shield**, the additional amount available to investors because of that deductibility [AP], calculated as `Tax shield = Rd × D × T`. The WACC with taxes is:

`WACC_after_tax = D% × Rd × (1 - T) + E% × Re`

This is lower than the pretax WACC, encouraging leverage use (Ch 17.4, "The Impact of Taxes").

### Optimal capital structure: trade-off theory

The interest tax shield grows with leverage, but **financial distress** also grows. Direct costs of financial distress include legal, consulting, appraisal, and auctioneer fees; indirect costs include loss of customers and suppliers (Ch 17.5, "Debt and Financial Distress"). **Trade-off theory** weighs the interest tax shield against the costs of financial distress; the optimal debt level is where the marginal benefit of additional tax shield equals the marginal cost of financial distress [AP] (Ch 17.5, "Trade-Off Theory"). Firms with higher costs of financial distress have lower optimal leverage.

A Link to Learning feature, "Netflix", describes a company that grew over 25 years from DVD rental to content streaming and then to a major producer of content [AE], "currently the largest media/entertainment company by market capitalization" [V]. Producing that content is expensive, and Netflix "has funded much of its content through selling debt" [V]. The feature points to the company's answers to common investor questions for its own explanation of this capital structure choice (Ch 17.5, "Netflix").

The chapter table (Ch 17.5, Table 17.7) shows substantial industry variation in capital structure. Online retailers average less than 7 per cent debt (6.67 per cent in the table), and computers/peripherals firms 8.55 per cent; rubber and tires firms average 63.62 per cent debt. These reflect industry-specific risks and the trade-off between tax shields and distress costs.

### Alternative sources of funds

**Preferred stock** has a fixed dividend, no maturity, no voting rights, and stands ahead of common stock in liquidation; its cost is `Rp = D / P` (Ch 17.6, "Preferred Shares"). Preferred dividends are after-tax payments by the issuer.

A Think It Through feature, "Calculating Common Equity Financing", estimates the WACC of Greene Building Company (40 per cent debt, 15 per cent preferred stock, 45 per cent common stock; bond YTM 7.2 per cent; preferred cost 9.17 per cent; a $3.15 dividend growing 3 per cent a year on a $32.25 share price; 21 per cent tax rate) at 9.47 per cent [AE]. It ranks the component costs by the order of claimants: debt is cheapest because debt holders are paid first and the interest tax shield lowers its effective cost; preferred shareholders, later in line, require more; and common shareholders, as residual claimants, "have the greatest amount of risk and require the highest rate of return" [V] (Ch 17.6, "Calculating Common Equity Financing").

**Convertible bonds** give the bondholder the option to convert the bond into a fixed number of common shares; the **conversion ratio** is the number of shares per bond. Convertible debt carries lower interest rates because of the option's value but dilutes existing shareholders if exercised; the lower interest expense compensates for the possibility of conversion (Ch 17.6, "Convertible Debt").

**Issuing new common stock** is the most expensive form of capital because of investor risk premium and **flotation costs** (filing fees, investment banker fees). Net proceeds from issuance are price minus flotation cost; the cost of new equity capital is `Re_new = D₁ / (P - F) + g`, where F is the flotation cost per share (Ch 17.6, "Issuing New Common Stock").

A Think It Through feature, "Cost of Issuing New Equity", works the point through for American Motor Works (AMW), with a target capital structure of 30 per cent debt and 70 per cent equity and an after-tax cost of debt of 4.6 per cent [AE]. Using retained earnings, the constant dividend growth model gives an equity cost of 12.57 per cent and a WACC of 10.18 per cent; $10 million of retained earnings plus $4,285,714 of new debt supports $14,285,714 of new financing at the target structure. Growth beyond that needs new stock (or a higher weight of debt), and new stock carries flotation costs, so a large project such as a new production facility means the company "will face a higher WACC than when using retained earnings as its equity financing" [V] (Ch 17.6, "Cost of Issuing New Equity").

## Part XVIII: Financial forecasting (Ch 18)

### Why forecast

Forecasts use historical data, analytical tools, and other contextual information to make educated guesses about future financial performance [AP] (Ch 18.1, "Financial Statement Foundations"). A budget is a static forecast (Ch 18, "Why It Matters"); after the formal budget, a rolling forecast is done monthly "to adjust as time moves on, more information becomes available, and circumstances change" [V] (Ch 18.3, "Length of a Forecast"). The text emphasises ethics in forecasting: "there can be tremendous pressure on management to perform, to deliver certain levels of profit, and to meet shareholder expectations . . . Forecasting . . . is not an exact science. There is a great deal of subjectivity that can come into play when forecasting sales and expenses. Ethical behavior is crucial in this area" [V] (Ch 18.1).

### Forecasting sales

Sales forecasts are the foundation; many other forecasts are derived from them [AP] (Ch 18.2, "Sales as the Driver"). Three steps:

1. Look at past data — typically the past 12 months of monthly data to identify seasonality and trends.
2. Use common-size and trend analyses on historical sales to project future totals.
3. Make qualitative adjustments based on what is known about the business, competitors, the economy, and customer demographics.

The text emphasises that "the past is not always a reliable predictor of the future" [V] (Ch 18.2, "Changes for the Future"). Sales-forecasting accuracy is improved by considering external factors (new competition, regulatory change, demographic shifts) and internal factors (new product lines, marketing campaigns, leadership changes).

A Think It Through feature, "Sales Forecast for Big 5 Sporting Goods", applies historical growth to a public company: net sales of $1,041,212,000 in 2020 against $996,495,000 in 2019 represent 4.5 per cent growth, so a 4.5 per cent forecast might be appropriate on that information alone, while many other factors should also be weighed [AE]. "Historical sales are only one set of data to use as a starting point" [V] (Ch 18.2, "Sales Forecast for Big 5 Sporting Goods").

### Pro forma financials

**Pro forma** financial statements are forward-looking; they use sales forecasts, historical data, and account relationships to project future statements [AP] (Ch 18.3, "Purpose of a Forecast"). One-year forecasts broken into monthly increments are typical for cash-flow planning; multi-year forecasts (typically quarterly or annual) are typical for strategic planning. **Variable costs** vary with sales (direct labour, direct materials); **fixed costs** do not change with sales within a relevant range (rent, salaries). Forecasting variable costs as a percentage of sales is appropriate; fixed costs are forecast as dollar amounts.

A Concepts in Practice feature, "COVID-19 Makes Forecasting Difficult for Big 5 Sporting Goods", draws on press and practitioner sources [BT, GlobeNewswire; Yahoo Finance; CPA Practice Advisor]. Big 5 Sporting Goods announced record earnings in the third quarter of 2020 and attributed them to people's reactions to the pandemic: people in quarantine still wanted to make healthy lifestyle choices, and sporting goods stores made record sales. Such sales are not certain to continue, and "The impacts of the pandemic are extremely difficult to predict" [V], which makes pro forma statements hard to assemble (Ch 18.3, "COVID-19 Makes Forecasting Difficult for Big 5 Sporting Goods").

### Generating the complete forecast

The **forecasted income statement** uses the sales forecast and historical relationships to project each line. Where future events are known (new compensation programs, lease changes, planned capital purchases), they override historical relationships (Ch 18.4, "Forecast the Income Statement"). The **forecasted balance sheet** is generated by linking accounts to the forecasted income statement: accounts receivable depend on sales and credit terms; inventory depends on cost of goods sold and inventory policy; accounts payable depend on cost of goods sold and payment terms; retained earnings depend on net income and dividend policy. Cash is typically the "plug" that balances the balance sheet (Ch 18.4, "Forecast the Balance Sheet").

### Cash flow forecast

A **cash forecast** begins with the beginning cash balance, adds anticipated cash inflows, and deducts anticipated cash outflows; this identifies surpluses and deficits month by month [AP] (Ch 18.5, "Create a Cash Flow Forecast"). Companies often have a target minimum cash balance (Clear Lake's example uses $35,000); deficits below this trigger short-term financing decisions.

### Scenarios and sensitivity analysis

**Scenario analysis** explores how multiple variable changes affect the financial outlook (a recession scenario versus a normal-economy scenario versus an expansion scenario) [AP] (Ch 18.5, "Scenarios in Forecasting"). **Sensitivity analysis** examines how output changes with one input at a time — useful for identifying which forecast inputs are most consequential (Ch 18.5, "Sensitivity Analysis in Forecasting"). Both are facilitated by spreadsheet software with linked formulas.

## Part XIX: Trade credit and working capital (Ch 19)

### Working capital basics

**Working capital** describes the resources needed to meet daily, weekly, and monthly operating cash flow needs [AP] (Ch 19.1, "What Is Working Capital?"). **Gross working capital** is current assets; **net working capital (NWC)** is current assets minus current liabilities. The goal of working capital management is to maintain adequate working capital to meet operational needs and current liabilities while not holding excessive (idle) assets that generate no return.

Three Think It Through features work through the liquidity ratios [AE]. In “Current Ratio”, $2,000,000 of current assets against $1,000,000 of current liabilities gives “a 2:1 proportion of current asset value to the amount of the current liabilities” [V]: if all current assets became cash, the current liabilities could be paid twice over [AE] (Ch 19.1, “Current Ratio”). In “Quick Ratio”, taking $500,000 of inventory out of the same current assets “would indicate a smaller cushion of net working capital” [V] (Ch 19.1, “Quick Ratio”). “Cash Ratio” calls the cash ratio “even more conservative” [V] because it counts only cash and marketable securities; with $1,100,000 of these against $1,000,000 of current liabilities, cash covers the current bills with $100,000 to spare [AE] (Ch 19.1, “Cash Ratio”).

The **operating cycle** is the time from inventory acquisition to sale; the **cash conversion cycle** extends this to receipt of cash from customers minus the time to pay suppliers (Ch 19.1, "The Cash Cycle"):

`Cash conversion cycle = Inventory conversion period + Receivables collection period − Payables deferral period`

Each component is calculated from the corresponding turnover ratio. Shortening the cycle frees up cash; lengthening it strains liquidity. The text takes a position on payables: "the payables deferral period is the one element that probably cannot be optimized without violating credit terms" [V] — paying suppliers on time preserves the relationship and credit rating (Ch 19.1).

The Think It Through feature “Periods of the Cash Cycle” applies the three period calculations to King Sized Products (KSP) Inc.: annual credit sales of $40,000,000, cost of goods sold of $30,000,000, average inventory of $3,000,000, average accounts receivable of $6,000,000 and average accounts payable of $2,800,000 give a cash cycle of 57.2 days [AE] (Ch 19.1, “Periods of the Cash Cycle”). Table 19.2 puts the three periods at 36.50, 54.75 and 34.07 days, and the follow-on feature shows lower inventory and receivables and higher payables cutting the cycle to 44.1 days with no change in sales [AE] (Ch 19.1, “The Cash Conversion Cycle”).

A Link to Learning feature points to a Harvard Business School blog post, “How Amazon Survived the Dot-Com Bubble” [BT, Harvard Business School]. Amazon managed its cash conversion cycle until it was “receiving payment for the things it sold before Amazon had to pay for them” [V], a negative cycle the text calls “really a huge positive for a company trying to manage positive cash flow” [V] (Ch 19.1, “How Amazon Survived the Dot-Com Bubble”).

Working capital needs vary by industry: home construction has very long cycles; restaurants can have very short or even negative cycles. Walmart's current ratio of around 0.9 is enabled by strong supply-chain management (Ch 19.1, "Working Capital Needs by Industry").

### Trade credit

**Trade credit** (accounts payable) is a vendor's extension of credit to a buyer; it is "spontaneous financing" that grows with sales [AP] (Ch 19.2, "How Trade Credit Works"). Trade credit is normally interest-free; **net terms** specify the credit period, and **cash discounts** offer incentives for early payment. Taking a quick-payment discount lowers the cost of what was bought: inventory for a manufacturer, retailer or wholesaler, and operating expenses for services bought on trade credit [AP] (Ch 19.2, “Trade Credit Terms”).

The annual cost of forgoing a quick-payment discount is given by the formula in the chapter (Ch 19.2, "Cost of Trade Credit"). The text's example: terms of 2/10 net 30 imply that not taking the discount costs 36.73 per cent on an annualised basis — far more than most firms pay for short-term financing.

### Cash management

Three motives for holding cash (Ch 19.3, "Motivations for Holding Cash"):

- **Transactional motive**: paying employees, vendors, creditors, dividends.
- **Precautionary motive**: emergencies and unexpected events.
- **Speculative motive**: ready availability for unexpected opportunities.

**Compensating balances** are minimum balances required by a bank in exchange for other corporate services. Excess cash is invested in **cash equivalents (cash alternatives)** — short-term, low-risk, highly liquid investments such as T-bills, federal agency securities, certificates of deposit, and commercial paper.

### Receivables and inventory management

Receivables management begins before the sale: can the customer be approved? what credit terms? what credit limit? Creditworthiness is judged by financial statements, financial ratios, and credit reports/scores (Ch 19.4). The **accounts receivable aging schedule** classifies outstanding receivables by age (how long past due); older receivables have higher uncollectibility percentages. Aging is used to estimate **bad debt expense** and the **allowance for doubtful accounts** (a contra-asset).

A Link to Learning feature, “Corporate Finance Institute”, names tools credit managers use to judge creditworthiness [BT, Corporate Finance Institute]. It quotes the institute’s website that “the ‘5 Cs of Credit’ is a common phrase used to describe the five major factors [character, capacity, collateral, capital, and conditions]” [V] used to judge a potential borrower, and that a credit report gives a full account of the borrower’s total debt, current balances, credit limits, and any history of defaults and bankruptcies [BT, Corporate Finance Institute] (Ch 19.4, “Corporate Finance Institute”).

Inventory management balances four cost components (Ch 19.5, "Inventory Cost"):

- **Purchasing costs**: the invoice amount.
- **Carrying costs**: storage, insurance, obsolescence, spoilage, opportunity cost of capital tied up.
- **Ordering costs**: the cost of placing orders.
- **Stockout costs**: lost sales when inventory is unavailable.

**Just-in-time (JIT)** inventory practices and **economic order quantity (EOQ)** are tools for minimising total inventory cost while meeting demand. **Lower of cost or market** is the GAAP requirement to mark inventory down when its market value falls below cost.

## Part XX: Risk management for the financial manager (Ch 20)

### Three areas of focus for the financial manager

Three focal areas for the financial manager (Ch 20.1, "What Is Risk?"): increase cash inflows and decrease cash outflows; speed up cash inflows and slow down cash outflows; decrease the riskiness of both inflows and outflows. Risk in finance is uncertainty — "risk occurs because you cannot predict the future" [V] (Ch 20.1, "What Is Risk?"). Hedging takes actions to reduce exposure to risk; speculating bets on future outcomes for profit. The text takes a position: "in finance, hedging is a risk management tool. . . Speculating . . . involves directional bets" [V] (Ch 20.1, "Risk and Firm Value"). The same tools serve both ends: "Many of these same strategies can be used by economic players who wish to speculate" [V]. The chapter sets its own scope: "the focus is on the perspective of a financial manager using these strategies to manage risk" [V] (Ch 20.1, "Risk and Firm Value").

### Commodity price risk

Three hedges for commodity price risk (Ch 20.2):

- **Long-term contracts** with suppliers lock in prices but expose both parties to default risk and reduce flexibility.
- **Vertical integration** merges a company with its supplier; the buyer's costs and the supplier's revenues are now internalised.
- **Futures contracts** are standardised, exchange-traded agreements to trade an asset on a future date at a price locked in today. Margin requirements and **marking to market** (daily exchange of cash flows based on price changes) reduce counterparty risk.

The Think It Through feature “The CME Group” notes that in 2007 the Chicago Mercantile Exchange merged with the Chicago Board of Trade to form CME Group Inc., which offers trading in futures and other contracts that companies can use to hedge risk [AP]; the rest of the feature points to a video on how futures on agricultural products, metals, energy and currencies are traded (Ch 20.2, “The CME Group”).

### Exchange rate risk

Three exchange-rate risks were introduced in Ch 3.5 and revisited (Ch 20.3, "Exchange Rate Risks"):

- **Transaction risk**: change in the value of expected receipts or expenses.
- **Translation risk**: change in the reported (book) value of foreign assets when consolidated into the home currency.
- **Economic risk**: change in customer base or sales because of relative purchasing-power changes — affects firms with no direct international transactions.

Hedges (Ch 20.3):

- **Futures contracts** for currencies (standardised, exchange-traded).
- **Forward contracts**, contractual agreements between two parties (often a firm and its bank) to exchange currencies on a future date at a forward rate. Forward contracts are flexible (any size, any date) but carry counterparty risk.
- **Natural hedges** offset risk through internal operations — a British travel agency selling Italian tours to British customers can offset that risk by selling London tours to euro-zone customers.

The Think It Through feature “Projecting Sales in US Dollars” shows transaction risk on the revenue side. A firm that expects JPY 50,000,000 of sales in Japan values them at USD 500,000 at its forecast exchange rate; at the actual rate in the example they are worth USD 415,000, so the firm “would receive $85,000 less from these sales in Japan than it was expecting” [V], even if it met its unit-sales goals [AE] (Ch 20.3, “Projecting Sales in US Dollars”).

### Options

A financial **option** "gives the owner the right, but not the obligation, to purchase or sell an asset for a specified price at some future date" [V] (Ch 20.3, "Options"). Options are **derivatives** — their value derives from another asset.

Terminology: the **strike price (exercise price)** is the price the holder pays/receives if exercising; the **premium** is the price paid for the option; the **expiration date** is when the option expires. **American options** can be exercised at any time up to expiration; **European options** only on expiration (the labels are unrelated to where they are traded).

Two main types (Ch 20.3):

- **Call option**: right to buy. Holder profits when the underlying price rises above strike + premium; option writer's loss is mirror image.
- **Put option**: right to sell. Holder profits when the underlying price falls below strike - premium; option writer's loss is mirror image.

The holder decides whether to exercise by comparing strike and spot at expiry: "It simply compares the strike price of KWN 1,200/USD to the market, or spot, exchange rate at the time the option is expiring" [V] (Ch 20.3, "Call Options"). Where spot lies between the strike and the strike adjusted for the premium, the holder still exercises and recovers part of the premium, though the net payoff is negative: in the call example, "the company will be 25 KWN worse off than if it had never purchased the call option" [V] (Ch 20.3, "Call Options"); in the put example, the company exercises and its payoff is INR -2 (Ch 20.3, "Put Options").

The text takes a position: option contracts are zero-sum games. The holder's gain equals the writer's loss and vice versa.

### Interest rate risk and swaps

When interest rates rise, the present value of future cash flows falls, including the price of fixed-coupon bonds. **Duration** is the standard measure of bond price sensitivity to interest rate changes; the chapter notes (without computing) that duration rises with longer maturity, lower coupon rate, and lower current yield [AP] (Ch 20.4, "Measuring Interest Rate Risk").

A **swap** involves two parties agreeing to exchange specified payment streams. The classic example is an interest rate swap: a high-rated firm (say, AAA) borrows at a fixed rate, while a lower-rated firm (BBB) borrows at a floating rate; they then swap, with the higher-rated firm paying floating to the lower-rated firm and the lower-rated firm paying fixed. Both firms benefit because their respective comparative advantages in fixed and floating markets are exploited (Ch 20.4, "Swap-Based Hedging"). In the worked example, Alpha (AAA) can borrow at a floating rate that comes to 3.0% when LIBOR is 2.75%, or at a fixed 5.0%; through the swap it is “said to have swapped its fixed interest rate for a floating rate” [V], taking on fluctuating rates that a AAA company “can withstand” [V], and it lowers its rate by 0.75%, while Beta fixes its rate at 6.25%, 0.5% below its 6.75% fixed-rate cost [AE] (Ch 20.4, "Swap-Based Hedging").

A Link to Learning feature, “LIBOR Transition”, notes that while the basic principles of financial transactions stay the same, the instruments in use change with innovation, regulation and technological advances, and that the use of LIBOR as a benchmark rate “is winding down in the early 2020s” [V] (Ch 20.4, “LIBOR Transition”). The main text adds that no single alternative benchmark has yet become the most used, so its swap example keeps LIBOR [AP] (Ch 20.4, "Swap-Based Hedging").

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- **Pure profit-as-goal thinking**. The text repeatedly distinguishes profit from cash flow and argues cash flow is the more reliable measure of business health. "Cash flow is the axis upon which the world of business spins" (Irina Simmons interview, Ch 9.1).
- **Use of payback period as a primary capital-budgeting criterion**. The text catalogues four disadvantages (ignores TVM, no theoretically grounded acceptance threshold, ignores cash flows after breakeven, no risk adjustment) and recommends NPV as the theoretically correct method (Ch 16.1).
- **IRR-only ranking of mutually exclusive projects**. The text takes the position that the highest-NPV project should be chosen, not the highest-IRR project, because IRR ignores scale and assumes intermediate cash flows reinvested at the IRR rate (Ch 16.5).
- **Treating SPACs as superior alternatives to IPOs from the public investor's perspective**. The Renaissance Capital study cited shows SPAC mergers averaging -18.8 per cent return vs +37.2 per cent for traditional IPOs (Ch 12.1).
- **Payday advance loans, refund anticipation loans, and similar short-term credit products**. The text explicitly highlights effective annual rates that can exceed 300 per cent on what appear to be modest fees (Ch 8.4).
- **Investing in non-investment-grade junk bonds without understanding their cyclical default behaviour**. The text notes 11 per cent of US junk bonds defaulted in 2001 and that the market had a brief resurgence in the late 1990s (Ch 10.4).
- **Trade credit as truly free**. Although trade credit is interest-free, the opportunity cost of forgoing cash discounts can be 36+ per cent annualised — the text frames not taking discounts as a substantial hidden expense (Ch 19.2).
- **Treating Excel's NPV function as computing the conventional NPV**. The text emphasises Excel's NPV starts with year-1 cash flows; the time-zero cash flow must be subtracted separately to get the conventional NPV (Ch 16.6).

Coverage is **substantive content only** per the v0.1.5 ingestion rule (Option B): chapter introductions and all numbered substantive sections are included; per-chapter pedagogical scaffolding (Summary, Key Terms, CFA Institute LOS cross-references, Multiple Choice, Review Questions, Problems, Video Activity) is excluded. Citation style is `(Ch N, "Section name")` because the conversion this reference was read from did not preserve PDF page anchors; section names provide stable citation anchors. Equation numbering in the text (e.g. "**3.1**", "**8.14**", "**17.7**") is preserved where it adds clarity but is not required for citation. The text's worked numerical examples (Bacon Signs, Clear Lake Sporting Goods, Bluebonnet Industries, Sam's Sporting Goods, Mayweather Inc., Lore Ltd., Maddox Inc.) are pedagogical fictional cases used by the authors to illustrate computations; they are referenced where they anchor a method but are not treated as empirical data.
